issues.legal_issue: A retrospective requirement that transfers of evacuee property be confirmed by the Custodian is a restriction on transfer rather than a deprivation of property, and its retrospective operation does not make it an unconstitutional deprivation.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired agricultural land from an evacuee before the relevant statute and its amendment came into force, and possession was transferred.
A later amendment applied from an earlier date and made transfers ineffective unless confirmed by the Custodian.
The purchaser sought confirmation, which was refused; the refusal deprived the purchaser of the benefit of the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The confirmation requirement was a reasonable restriction on transfers, not a deprivation of property, and its retrospective operation did not violate the asserted fundamental right.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution, the confirmation requirement for future transfers is a restriction on transfer rather than a deprivation of property. In light of the purpose and policy of evacuee-property law and the abnormal conditions from which it arose, that restriction is reasonable. Retrospective operation does not convert a restriction into a deprivation. The provision considered was section 5-A of the East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, as amended; no earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.fundamental_rights_petition: A person brings a proceeding seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.retrospective_confirmation_requirement_a: A later legal requirement for official confirmation is applied retrospectively to a transfer of property treated as evacuee property.

issues.definition: When a fundamental-rights proceeding concerns a retrospective confirmation requirement applied to a transfer of evacuee property, the rule treats that requirement as a reasonable restriction rather than a property deprivation.

issues.legal_issue: An allegedly illegal quasi-judicial refusal based on irrelevant material, without a violation of a fundamental right, does not support an application for enforcement of fundamental rights.
material_facts: The purchaser applied for confirmation of the transfer, and an Assistant Custodian recommended confirmation after finding the transaction genuine.
The Additional Custodian refused confirmation by relying on a Custodian-General circular establishing a policy against confirming transactions involving agricultural property.
The refusal was affirmed in revision, and the purchaser alleged that reliance on the circular was illegal and irrelevant.
issues.conclusion: Even if reliance on the circular was illegal, that alleged error did not itself establish a violation of a fundamental right, so the application for enforcement of fundamental rights was misconceived.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights; an alleged error in a quasi-judicial decision, including reliance on irrelevant material, does not by itself raise a question of fundamental-rights violation. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.fundamental_rights_petition: A person brings a proceeding seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.quasi_judicial_confirmation_refusal: An authority makes a quasi-judicial decision refusing to confirm a property transfer.
predicates.challenge_alleges_only_illegal_decision_: The applicant alleges that the authority relied on an improper or irrelevant basis, without establishing an independent infringement of a fundamental right.

issues.definition: When a fundamental-rights proceeding challenges a quasi-judicial refusal only for an allegedly illegal decision basis, the rule denies the remedy unless a fundamental-rights violation is established.
